title: Diamond Optomechanical Crystals For High-frequency Strain And Comb Generation
authors: Elham Zohari, Waleed El-Sayed, Aria Jafari, Ahmas El-Hamamsy, Peyman Parsa, Joseph E. Losby, Nat\'alia C. Carvalho, Paul E. Barclay
abstract: ArXiv:2608.27581v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum optomechanical technologies benefit from mechanical oscillators that are high-frequency, can be coherently driven, and are capable of coupling to other quantum systems. Diamond supports all of these criteria: its large elastic modulus increases mechanical resonance frequency, its low nonlinear optical absorption increases the allowed intensity of fields used for coherent optomechanics, and it hosts spin qubits that interact with mechanical modes. Here we demonstrate a diamond optomechanical crystal cavity that supports multiple mechanical resonances with [MATH]12 GHz frequency and high [MATH] product that can be coherently coupled to multiple optical modes. By exciting this sideband resolved system into mechanical self-sustained oscillations, we generate a frequency comb spanning 143 GHz. Analysis of the comb spectrum, combined with systematic characterization of the system's optomechanical coupling, allows us to quantitatively show that its mechanical oscillation amplitude reaches 130 pm. This corresponds to a maximum total dynamic strain of [MATH] that is sufficiently high for future demonstrations of optomechanical control of diamond spin qubits.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a diamond optomechanical crystal cavity that supports high-frequency mechanical resonances and generates a broad frequency comb via self-sustained oscillations, with potential for coupling to diamond spin qubits.
motivation: The goal is to develop high-frequency, coherently drivable mechanical oscillators that can couple to quantum systems, particularly diamond spin qubits, for quantum optomechanics applications.
method: The authors fabricated a diamond optomechanical crystal cavity, characterized its optical and mechanical modes, and excited it into mechanical self-sustained oscillations to generate a frequency comb. They analyzed the comb spectrum and optomechanical coupling to extract mechanical amplitude.
result: The device exhibits multiple mechanical resonances at ~12 GHz with high Q product, and generates a comb spanning 143 GHz. The mechanical oscillation amplitude is 130 pm, corresponding to a dynamic strain of ~10^-6.
conclusion: These results demonstrate that diamond optomechanical crystals can achieve sufficient strain for future optomechanical control of diamond spin qubits, advancing hybrid quantum systems.

title: Network Steering With Arbitrarily Low Detection Efficiency Of Any Entangled Measurement
authors: Shubhayan Sarkar
abstract: ArXiv:2608.27582v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum nonlocality and its asymmetric counterpart, quantum steering, are among the most intriguing manifestations of quantum mechanics. From a theoretical perspective, they are not only of fundamental significance but also hold promise for a wide range of applications. However, the stringent technological requirements for their experimental observation in a loophole-free way have largely restricted their realization to foundational demonstrations. A major challenge in these setups is the limited detection efficiency of current detectors as to observe nonlocality or steering in the standard scenarios, one requires detectors above a certain critical efficiency which can only be achieved with superconducting detectors. Considering the simplest quantum network, we demonstrate here that quantum steering between two parties, can be demonstrated for any non-zero detection efficiency, if the sources in the network generate states above a critical visibility well-within the current practical limits. This form of quantum steering in networks, is termed swap-steering. Moreover, when the sources are perfect, swap-steering can be observed using any entangled measurement on the untrusted side, even with arbitrarily low detection efficiency. Consequently, two major loopholes, the detection-loophole as well as free-will loophole can be closed easily in quantum steering experiments, when implemented using networks.
tldr: This paper demonstrates that quantum steering can be observed with arbitrarily low detection efficiency using swap-steering in a quantum network, provided the sources have sufficient visibility, closing major loopholes.
motivation: Detection efficiency limitations hinder loophole-free steering demonstrations; standard scenarios require high-efficiency detectors. The goal is to overcome these practical constraints using network configurations.
method: The authors consider the simplest quantum network and show that with imperfect sources above a critical visibility, swap-steering is possible at any non-zero detection efficiency. When sources are perfect, any entangled measurement on the untrusted side works even with arbitrarily low efficiency.
result: They prove that swap-steering can be observed for any non-zero detection efficiency under practical visibility conditions, and with perfect sources, even arbitrarily low detection efficiency suffices.
conclusion: This provides a practical route to loophole-free steering demonstrations, closing both detection and free-will loopholes, and advancing quantum information applications.

title: Difference Equations Of Average Entropies
authors: Youyi Huang, Linfeng Wei, Lu Wei, Peter J. Forrester
abstract: ArXiv:2608.27829v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Exact cumulants of entanglement entropies of random state ensembles have traditionally been studied within the random matrix framework. In this work, we propose an alternative approach based on the intrinsic connection to integrable systems. The central idea is to embed entropic quantities into tau functions satisfying Toda-type lattice equations, which in turn yield linear difference equations for their averages. Directly solving the difference equations recovers exact entropy formulas in the literature. The integrable systems approach bypasses the case-by-case, ensemble-dependent derivations required by random matrix methods. The approach also suggests a possible route towards unified and more efficient higher-order cumulant calculations by exploring integrable hierarchies.
tldr: This paper presents an integrable systems approach to compute cumulants of entanglement entropies for random state ensembles, using tau functions and Toda lattice equations.
motivation: Traditional random matrix methods require case-by-case derivations for different ensembles; the authors aim to provide a unified and more efficient method using integrable systems.
method: They embed entropic quantities into tau functions satisfying Toda-type lattice equations, which lead to linear difference equations for averages, and solve them directly.
result: Solving the difference equations recovers exact entropy formulas from the literature, demonstrating the effectiveness of the approach.
conclusion: The integrable systems approach offers a unified and efficient way to compute higher-order cumulants, potentially advancing the study of entanglement entropies in random states.

title: Predicting Multipartite Entanglement In Quantum Circuits Using Transformer
authors: Darell Timothy Tarigan, Fadhil Fatih Shiddiq, Hadyan Luthfan Prihadi, Donny Dwiputra, Jusak S. Kosasih, Yanoar P. Sarwono, Freddy Permana Zen, Rui-Qin Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2608.27993v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multipartite entanglement is a critical property of parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs), particularly for near-term hybrid quantum-classical algorithms, as it characterizes their ability to generate highly entangled states. However, measuring entanglement remains computationally expensive because conventional Monte Carlo sampling scales unfavorably with system size. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a graph-based transformer surrogate that predicts both the first-order Meyer-Wallach measure ([MATH]) and the second-order Scott measure ([MATH]), resolving entanglement structures indistinguishable under [MATH] alone. Our central contribution is the qubit-interconnected graph (QIG) encoding for transformers, where each node represents a qubit and weighted adjacencies record entangling-gate multiplicities. Fused with a gate-level DAG encoder, this yields the QIG-Fusion model. Evaluated on 50,000 circuits spanning 4- to 8-qubit systems across a ten-seed protocol, QIG-Fusion achieves an RMSE as low as 0.037 ([MATH]) and 0.038 ([MATH]), with a Spearman rank correlation up to 0.95. This framework significantly reduces the computational cost of Quantum Architecture Search (QAS), enabling efficient entanglement estimation for large-scale PQCs.
tldr: This paper introduces a transformer-based surrogate model, QIG-Fusion, to predict multipartite entanglement measures in parameterized quantum circuits, significantly reducing computational cost for quantum architecture search.
motivation: Measuring multipartite entanglement in quantum circuits is computationally expensive with conventional Monte Carlo sampling, especially for large systems, and existing measures like Meyer-Wallach alone are insufficient to resolve all entanglement structures.
method: The proposed QIG-Fusion model uses a qubit-interconnected graph (QIG) encoding where nodes represent qubits and weighted edges represent entangling-gate multiplicities, combined with a gate-level DAG encoder, and is trained on a large dataset of circuits.
result: On 50,000 circuits with 4-8 qubits, QIG-Fusion achieves RMSE as low as 0.037 and 0.038 for the first and second-order measures respectively, with Spearman rank correlation up to 0.95.
conclusion: The framework provides efficient entanglement estimation for large-scale PQCs, facilitating practical quantum architecture search by reducing computational overhead.

title: Error-Adaptive Quasi-local Decoding Of The Toric Code
authors: Hossein Dehghani, Sarang Gopalakrishnan, Michael Gullans
abstract: ArXiv:2608.27740v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Topological quantum memories need decoders that are both reliable and scalable, but these goals compete: globally informed decoders are accurate near threshold yet expensive, while strictly local rules are fast but can miss long-range structure. Motivated by recent recoverability and mixed-state viewpoints, we make this tradeoff operational for the dephased toric code through a decoder-level local recoverability diagnostic. We compare global MWPM corrections to quasi-local corrections inside a target region and define a matching ratio [MATH], with mismatch [MATH]. Across geometry families, [MATH] shows strong buffer-controlled suppression and is well organized by a two-geometry scaling form. For scaled families, especially [MATH], [MATH] exhibits a clear crossing and finite-size collapse near [MATH], consistent with a growing recoverability scale near the decoding transition. We use this scaling to formulate an adaptive buffer-selection rule and to identify a distance-scaled initialization for a composite quasi-local RG decoder on the full torus. In the tuned family [MATH], the resulting logical-failure curves show an apparent finite-size crossing at [MATH]--[MATH], below the conventional MWPM threshold scale. We focus on dephasing noise with perfect syndrome measurements to cleanly isolate the underlying behavior.

title: Quantized Low-Rank Quantum State Tomography: Hyperbolic Quantization And Riemannian Least-Squares Recovery
authors: Hanqin Cai, Longxiu Huang, Juntao You
abstract: ArXiv:2608.27503v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study low-rank quantum state tomography from finite-bit Pauli batch responses. title: From Integrability To Many-body Quantum Chaos Through A Markovian Bath
authors: Antonio M. Garc\'ia-Garc\'ia Xianlong Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2608.27897v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent examples have confirmed the common belief that quantum chaos is always suppressed in the presence of an environment. Here we show that this is not always the case. We compute the Lyapunov exponent of a [MATH]-body Majorana Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model coupled to a Markovian bath. Explicit analytical results are obtained in the [MATH] and large [MATH] limits. Our results put forward an alternate route to induce and control the generation of scrambling in quantum many-body systems which is of potential relevance in the design of quantum information devices.

title: The Thermodynamic Freedom Of A Thermodynamic Computer

abstract: ArXiv:2608.27938v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Thermodynamic computers are stochastic physical devices designed to perform calculations at the thermal energy scale. These results indicate that a thermodynamic computer designed for a particular task retains considerable freedom in its thermodynamic operation.

title: Physics-Constrained Conditional Generative Learning For Quantum State And Process Tomography
authors: Daming Li
abstract: ArXiv:2608.28035v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum state and process tomography constitute essential diagnostic tools in quantum information science, yet their standard formulations suffer from prohibitive computational scaling as the number of qubits grows. In this work, we introduce a physics-constrained conditional generative adversarial network that bypasses iterative constrained inversion by directly learning a forward generative mapping conditioned on Pauli expectation values. The generator embeds a differentiable Cholesky layer at its output, which enforces Hermiticity, positive semidefiniteness, and unit trace by construction. Our experiments reveal that the strength of the [MATH] penalty critically governs the emergence of GHZ coherence during training: an excessively large penalty postpones the coherence onset and yields a prolonged low-fidelity plateau, whereas an intermediate value enables the fastest stable convergence. Moreover, for high-temperature thermal states, an over-complete measurement basis proves necessary to prevent sustained late-stage fluctuations. By extending the same Cholesky constraint to the Choi-matrix representation, the framework naturally accommodates quantum process tomography. For systems with [MATH] qubits, the exponential growth of the underlying [MATH] density matrix remains the fundamental bottleneck; we discuss how integrating tensor-network structures can contain the per-iteration cost while preserving reconstruction fidelity. Altogether, these results suggest that physically constrained generative learning offers a scalable and amortizable pathway toward data-driven tomography for noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices.
tldr: The paper introduces a physics-constrained conditional GAN for scalable quantum state and process tomography.
motivation: Standard tomography scales poorly with qubit number, limiting its applicability to large quantum systems.
method: A conditional GAN is used with a generator that incorporates a differentiable Cholesky layer to enforce Hermiticity, positive semidefiniteness, and unit trace; the approach is extended to process tomography via the Choi matrix.
result: The penalty strength significantly affects convergence, with an optimal value enabling stable convergence; over-complete measurement bases are necessary for high-temperature thermal states. Tensor-network integration is identified as a potential further improvement.
conclusion: Physically constrained generative learning offers a scalable and amortizable pathway for tomography on noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices.

title: Quantifying The Dual-isotope Advantage For Ytterbium-array Surface Codes Using Realistic Noise Models
authors: Fumiyoshi Kobayashi, Toshi Kusano, Nicholas Fazio, Yuma Nakamura
abstract: ArXiv:2608.27568v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neutral-atom quantum computers are a promising platform for fault-tolerant quantum computation, but logical performance depends on systemic realistic noise factors during syndrome extraction. In dual-isotope Yb arrays, the roles of data and ancilla qubits are separated spectrally, allowing ancilla qubits to be measured in place without additional transport or shelving operations. Here we quantify the advantage of a dual-isotope Yb architecture for surface code memories. We develop an experimentally motivated Clifford-compatible noise model for dual-isotope 171Yb-174Yb systems using generalised Pauli twirling and implement it as a wrapper for Stim called DualYbSim, which has been packaged as an open source Python library. Simulations of rotated and XZZX surface codes show that a dual-isotope architecture with in-place measurement achieves the lowest logical error rates among the architectures considered, outperforming single-isotope schemes based on shelving or zoned measurement. Our error-budget analysis also identifies Rydberg-state decay as the dominant limitation, contributing to 74-80% of the logical error rate scaling, highlighting concrete experimental targets for improving FTQC performance.
tldr: This paper presents a simulation study quantifying the performance advantage of dual-isotope ytterbium-array architectures for surface code error correction under realistic noise conditions.
motivation: The motivation is to evaluate whether dual-isotope Yb arrays offer practical benefits for fault-tolerant quantum computing by reducing logical error rates, and to identify the dominant noise sources limiting performance.
method: The authors develop a Clifford-compatible noise model for 171Yb-174Yb systems using generalized Pauli twirling, implement it as a Stim wrapper named DualYbSim, and simulate rotated and XZZX surface codes across several measurement architectures.
result: Simulations show that the dual-isotope architecture with in-place measurement yields the lowest logical error rates, outperforming single-isotope schemes. An error-budget analysis identifies Rydberg-state decay as the dominant limitation, accounting for 74-80% of the logical error rate scaling.
conclusion: The results provide concrete experimental targets for improving fault-tolerant quantum computation, particularly mitigating Rydberg-state decay, and suggest dual-isotope Yb arrays as a promising platform for surface code implementations.

abstract: ArXiv:2608.27679v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deterministic Secure Quantum Communication (DSQC) is a quantum cryptographic technique engineered to transfer a message through a quantum channel, requiring an auxiliary classical channel for eavesdropping verification and decoding, but without prior key distribution. This article presents a theoretical high-dimensional prepare and measure DSQC protocol using the Reed-Solomon erasure coding to ensure data resilience to noise. This protocol offers the following benefits: it eliminates the need for quantum memory or entanglement, it can be built with commercially available technology, and its higher capacity improves the overall transmission rate.

title: Logical Neural Belief Propagation For Linear-Complexity Decoding Of Surface Codes
authors: Hee-Youl Kwak, Seong-Joon Park, Dae-Young Yun, Eliya Nachmani, Jae-Won Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2608.27682v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum error correction (QEC) requires decoders that achieve high logical accuracy while scaling efficiently with the code length. Belief propagation (BP) is attractive for its linear decoding complexity, but conventional BP decoders often fail to reach sufficient logical accuracy on surface codes. We propose Logical Neural Belief Propagation (L-NBP), a BP-based neural decoder that redirects the decoding objective from physical-level decoding to logical-level decoding. L-NBP first runs a neural BP (NBP) module that produces posterior beliefs, and a logical classifier then transforms these beliefs into a continuous-valued soft syndrome and predicts the logical operator. Because all components in L-NBP are trainable by backpropagation, L-NBP is trained end-to-end, so that the NBP module learns to extract soft syndromes that are favorable for logical classification. On surface codes, L-NBP matches or outperforms the BP with ordered-statistics decoding (BP-OSD) and minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) while retaining the linear complexity of BP, and achieves a threshold of [MATH] under depolarizing noise. Moreover, under circuit-level noise, L-NBP matches the accuracy of BP-OSD on the distance-[MATH] surface code while requiring only [MATH] of its complexity. These results show that combining BP, neural weights, and logical-level decoding enables scalable and high-accuracy quantum decoding.

motivation: Belief propagation decoders for surface codes are efficient but often inaccurate; there is a need for a decoder that combines linear complexity with high logical accuracy.
method: L-NBP runs a neural BP module to produce posterior beliefs, which are then transformed by a logical classifier into a continuous soft syndrome to predict the logical operator; all components are trained end-to-end via backpropagation.
result: On surface codes, L-NBP matches or outperforms BP-OSD and MWPM with linear complexity, achieving a threshold under depolarizing noise and matching BP-OSD accuracy under circuit-level noise at reduced complexity.
conclusion: Combining BP, neural weights, and logical-level decoding enables scalable and high-accuracy quantum error correction for surface codes.

title: Hybrid Heralded Noiseless Amplification With Finite-Cutoff Quantum Scissors

abstract: ArXiv:2608.27872v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A noiseless linear amplifier (NLA) can probabilistically amplify an optical state without the noise required by deterministic phase-insensitive amplification. title: High-Throughput Normalized Min-Sum Belief Propagation Decoding For Quantum Ldpc Codes With Near-Memory Processing
authors: Jeonggeun Seo, Youngsun Han, Leanghok Hour, Dongmin Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2608.27901v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Real-time quantum error correction requires classical decoders to process growing syndrome workloads with low and predictable latency. For quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes, iterative belief propagation (BP) repeatedly updates messages over sparse Tanner graphs, creating substantial memory-access and data-movement demands. We map normalized Min-Sum BP decoding of the [[144,12,12]] Bivariate Bicycle qLDPC code onto a DPU-based Processing-in-Memory (PIM) architecture. Within each DPU, 11 tasklets cooperatively decode one syndrome, while multiple DPUs process independent syndrome instances in parallel. Using uPIMulator and a data-qubit Pauli error model with ideal syndrome measurements, we compare throughput, per-syndrome processing time, logical error rate (LER), and single-syndrome tail latency against a 16-logical-CPU baseline. At a component-wise physical error probability of p=0.001 and one BP iteration, the projected aggregate kernel throughput of 2,560 DPUs reaches 1.071 x 10^7 decodes/s, compared with 1.22 x 10^6 decodes/s for the CPU, an 8.8x improvement. From two iterations onward, the measured LER remains below the physical error probability for every evaluated value of p. For one to five iterations, the maximum sampled serialized X+Z DPU compute latency remains below the 1 ms decoder-side reference for trapped-ion QEC, reaching approximately 0.873 ms at five iterations. These results show that near-memory processing can provide high aggregate throughput and sub-millisecond compute latency for qLDPC BP decoding under the evaluated conditions.

authors: Dzung Quoc Ngo, Tharmikka Raveendranathan, Tuan Anh Le, Vinod Sharma, Purav Shah, Huan X. Nguyen
abstract: ArXiv:2608.28480v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Open Radio Access Networks (O-RAN) introduce unprecedented flexibility, interoperability, and intelligence into next-generation wireless systems, but their disaggregated and software-defined architecture also expands the attack surface and creates new security vulnerabilities. Their integration with the Near-Real-Time (Near-RT) RAN Intelligent Controller, O-Cloud, and open interfaces is analyzed, together with practical deployment considerations, technology maturity, and adoption timelines. Finally, open research directions are outlined toward secure, resilient, and future-proof O-RAN architectures for 6G networks.

title: Reverse Quantum Mechanics
authors: Gabriele Carcassi, Tobias Thrien, Christine A. Aidala
abstract: ArXiv:2608.27543v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reverse Physics is a methodology that breaks physical theories into separate mathematical and physical conditions to establish their logical relationships. To showcase the power of the methodology, we present several results for quantum mechanics and their related insights. The standard Hilbert-space formulation conflicts with basic physical requirements, while a minimal topological modification can solve these problems. The ensemble space, rather than the pure-state space, distinguishes classical from quantum systems. The Born rule is an additional assumption linking orthogonality, mutual exclusivity and information entropy. Under explicit background conditions, unitary evolution is equivalent to deterministic and reversible evolution. Nonselective projective measurements can be characterized as Lindblad equilibration processes, while unitary evolution can be characterized as a limit of infinitesimal projective processes. Classical mechanics is recovered as the high-entropy limit of quantum mechanics, and every quantum state, pure or mixed, is a dynamical, spectral and thermodynamic equilibrium. These results are self-contained, use the standard vector-space representation and can thus be used as common tools and constraints for teaching, interpretations, reconstructions and future theories.

title: Quantum Resource Estimation For Simulating The Syk Model With Trotterization, qDRIFT, And Asymmetric Qubitization
authors: Brian Goldsmith, Larissa Kroell, Nishna Aerabati
abstract: ArXiv:2608.27573v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model has been identified as a promising candidate to run on early fault-tolerant quantum computers due to the relatively modest resources required to probe non-trivial physics (namely holographic duality and AdS/CFT correspondence). As such, it is crucial that the details of how to run such a simulation are well understood. Using PsiQuantum's Construct platform, we implement and analyze three different approaches to simulate the SYK model: Trotterization, qDRIFT, and asymmetric qubitization with Quantum Signal Processing. We provide an open-source library containing implementations for SYK simulation using all three methods, which we use to obtain quantum resource estimates for qubit and T gate count as functions of the number of Majorana modes and precision. We find that while qDRIFT and Trotterization benefit from a lower qubit count, the large number of T gates required lead to asymmetric qubitization being advantageous in most cases. This reinforces previous theoretical considerations. We intend both the implementations and the estimates to be useful for researchers to continue to study the SYK model and understand how the techniques and resources vary.
tldr: Presents quantum resource estimates for simulating the SYK model using Trotterization, qDRIFT, and asymmetric qubitization, finding the latter advantageous in most cases.
motivation: To provide detailed resource estimates for simulating the SYK model on early fault-tolerant quantum computers, as it is a promising candidate for exploring holographic duality.
method: Implementations of three Hamiltonian simulation methods using PsiQuantum's Construct platform, with quantitative analysis of qubit and T gate counts as functions of Majorana modes and precision.
result: Asymmetric qubitization requires more qubits but significantly fewer T gates, making it advantageous over Trotterization and qDRIFT for most error targets.
conclusion: The open-source library and resource estimates enable further research on SYK simulation and comparison of simulation techniques.

title: Topological Winding Readout Of An Emergent Page-Wootters Clock
authors: Hesam Zaravashan, Gabriele Gradoni, Mohsen Khalily
abstract: ArXiv:2608.27650v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Page--Wootters construction gives time a Hilbert space, representing it as an internal degree of freedom whose readings the rest of the system evolves with respect to. We ask whether such a clock degree of freedom can carry a topological invariant, and we propose a photonic architecture in which it does and in which the invariant can be measured. Signal--idler pairs from spontaneous four-wave mixing in a coupled microring array supply the clock--system partition, with the idler occupying a Rice--Mele band whose staggered coupling and detuning are cycled adiabatically around a gap-closing point. One cycle acts on that band as a rigid translation by \(C\) unit cells, times a geometric phase periodic in the crystal momentum, times a dynamical phase, an identity exact in the adiabatic limit and independent of the state on which it acts. The readout targets the winding of that geometric phase across the Brillouin zone. Reversing the traversal of the pump loop cancels the dynamical phase and isolates twice the geometric phase in a two-photon coincidence fringe, while energy anticorrelation lets a filter on the signal scan the clock momentum without touching the clock and supplies the phase reference relationally, in place of an external optical reference. The estimate is protected on two independent levels, by the gap against smooth deformation and by the digital character of the unwrapping against noise below a threshold. A parameter budget anchored to thin-film lithium niobate places the requirements within reach at a conservative operating point.
tldr: This paper proposes a photonic architecture to realize an emergent Page-Wootters clock and measure a topological winding invariant using two-photon coincidence.
motivation: The Page-Wootters construction represents time as an internal degree of freedom, and the authors explore whether such a clock can carry a topological invariant, proposing a feasible photonic setup to measure it.
method: Signal-idler pairs from spontaneous four-wave mixing in a coupled microring array create the clock-system partition, with the idler in a Rice-Mele band adiabatically cycled around a gap-closing point; the readout uses two-photon coincidence fringes to isolate the geometric phase.
result: The proposed scheme cancels dynamical phase and isolates twice the geometric phase, with protection by the gap and digital unwrapping; a parameter budget indicates feasibility with thin-film lithium niobate.
conclusion: This work offers a new approach to measure topological invariants of a Page-Wootters clock, potentially impacting quantum foundations and topological photonics.

title: Efficient Quantum Simulation Of Variable-Coefficient Transport With Continuous Source Injection
authors: Mohammad Mehedi Hasan Akash, Turag Dev, Nhat-Quang Nguyen, Yanzhu Chen, Huixuan Wu, Kourosh Shoele
abstract: ArXiv:2608.27712v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum time-marching algorithms for transport PDEs often represent variable coefficients and forcing through register-expanding dilations, block-encoding oracles, or repeated postselection. We present an alternative algorithm for a forced variable-coefficient advection-diffusion equation in flow-inspired skew-symmetric form that incorporates spatially varying velocity, viscous dissipation, and persistent source injection with a peak logical requirement of [MATH] qubits. A centered skew-symmetric discretization makes the advection operator strictly skew-Hermitian for arbitrary velocity profiles, enabling an ancilla-free unitary realization using a Gray-code Trotter sequence of controlled-[MATH] rotations. Diffusion is applied in the Fourier basis through a uniformly controlled rotation on one postselected ancilla, which is measured, reset, and reused between the two diffusion half-steps, while the source is incorporated classically through second-order Strang splitting. Statevector simulations for [MATH] and [MATH] recover second-order temporal convergence against high-accuracy classical solutions, while Richardson extrapolation gives fourth-order accuracy and reduces kernel calls by factors of four to fourteen. Independent tests through [MATH] confirm second-order spatial consistency. We further show that the per-step ancilla failure probability is proportional to the instantaneous viscous dissipation rate, making postselection cost self-regulating over a fifty-fold viscosity range. Stable evolution is demonstrated for [MATH] time steps without observable secular error growth, while Gray-code advection accounts for [MATH]--[MATH] of transpiled controlled-NOT gates. The fixed-width kernel provides a qubit-efficient building block for near-term hardware studies, although classical readout and state re-preparation remain the main obstacles to coherent multistep evolution.
tldr: Presents a qubit-efficient quantum algorithm for simulating forced variable-coefficient advection-diffusion equations using Gray-code Trotter sequences and postselected ancilla.
motivation: To enable efficient quantum simulation of transport PDEs with variable coefficients and sources, reducing qubit overhead and improving stability.
method: Uses a skew-symmetric discretization for ancilla-free advection, Fourier-domain diffusion with a reused postselected ancilla, and Strang splitting for source terms.
result: Statevector simulations show second-order temporal convergence, fourth-order via Richardson extrapolation, and stable evolution over long times with self-regulating postselection failure.
conclusion: Provides a scalable building block for near-term quantum hardware, though classical readout and state re-preparation remain challenges.

title: Benchmarking Quantum Feature Encoding Strategies For Binary Classification With Qsvm
authors: Murat Kurt
abstract: ArXiv:2608.27764v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The way in which classical data are encoded into quantum states plays a significant role in both classification performance and quantum circuit complexity in Quantum Machine Learning. In this study, the effects of different quantum feature encoding strategies on Quantum Support Vector Machine performance were investigated using five binary classification datasets. In particular, the statistical relationships between features were incorporated into quantum circuits through \(RY(\theta)\) and controlled-\(RY(\theta)\) gates, and this approach was compared with conventional quantum feature maps. The results demonstrate that incorporating statistical relationships into the encoding process can influence classification performance. However, more complex and densely entangled circuits do not necessarily yield higher performance. In addition, a composite evaluation metric was employed to jointly assess predictive performance, generalization, and circuit cost. The findings across the five datasets indicate that the choice of quantum feature encoding strategy should account for the underlying structure of the data and that predictive performance should be evaluated together with quantum circuit complexity.
tldr: This paper benchmarks various quantum feature encoding strategies for binary classification using quantum support vector machines, finding that incorporating statistical relationships between features can influence performance but increased circuit complexity does not guarantee better results.
motivation: The choice of feature encoding in quantum machine learning significantly impacts both classification performance and circuit complexity, yet systematic comparisons are lacking.
method: The author tested conventional quantum feature maps and encoding circuits using RY and controlled-RY gates to incorporate statistical feature relationships, across five binary classification datasets, using a composite metric that balances predictive performance, generalization, and circuit cost.
result: Encoding that incorporates statistical relationships between features can affect performance, but more complex and densely entangled circuits do not necessarily yield higher performance; optimal strategy depends on data structure.
conclusion: The selection of quantum feature encoding should consider the underlying data structure and evaluate predictive performance together with quantum circuit complexity.

title: Self-partitioned Interfacial Time Crystals
authors: Yi Yang Joseph Huang
abstract: ArXiv:2608.28126v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nonequilibrium many-body systems can spontaneously break symmetry in time, as in time crystals, or in space, through self-organized domains and interfaces. Whether these two forms of symmetry breaking can intertwine so that an emergent interface alone hosts time-crystalline order remains unknown. In this work, by introducing the Rabi-Hatano-Nelson model, we unveil the existence and mechanism of a self-partitioned interfacial time crystal (SPITC), where a homogeneous system generates its own internal and tunable interface, at which the time-translation symmetry is also spontaneously broken. Such a SPITC phase is intrinsically induced by nonreciprocity and open boundary conditions, without external pumping or long-range interaction. The periodic and open boundary phase diagrams of the system are both mapped out; vacuum and Dicke-like superradiance with static or active orders are identified, with analytical phase boundaries in the weak coupling limit. The frequency of the SPITC is found to scale quadratically with the spin-photon coupling strength, as we derive analytically for the slow dynamics of the spins. The position of the SPITC boundary scales with a critical exponent of [MATH] as a function of the degree of nonreciprocity, in stark contrast to [MATH] for an otherwise stationary boundary. Our construction of SPITC establishes a route to spatiotemporal order in non-Hermitian many-body systems.
tldr: The paper introduces the Rabi-Hatano-Nelson model and demonstrates a self-partitioned interfacial time crystal (SPITC) phase where an emergent interface spontaneously breaks time-translation symmetry in a homogeneous non-Hermitian system.
motivation: To investigate whether time-translation symmetry breaking can occur at an emergent interface, combining temporal and spatial symmetry breaking in a many-body system without external driving or long-range interactions.
method: The authors propose the Rabi-Hatano-Nelson model, which incorporates nonreciprocity and open boundary conditions, and analyze its phase diagrams using analytical methods in the weak coupling limit and numerical approaches.
result: They identify a SPITC phase with tunable interface position and scale invariance, where the frequency scales quadratically with spin-photon coupling and the boundary position shows a critical exponent different from stationary boundaries.
conclusion: The work establishes a new route to spatiotemporal order in non-Hermitian many-body systems, showing that interfaces can autonomously host time-crystalline behavior.

title: Finite Sample Bounds For Composite Hypothesis Testing
authors: Amedeo Roberto Esposito El{\'i}as Vera-Sig{\"u}enza
abstract: ArXiv:2608.28068v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate composite binary hypothesis testing in the finite sample regime under asymmetric error constraints. Using R\'enyi divergences, we derive explicit achievability and converse bounds for the optimal Type II error. When the Type I error is constrained to decay exponentially with sample size, the bounds identify a phase transition and yield a strong converse above it. In the composite problem, the phase transition threshold is given by the joint KL projection over the alternative and null classes. Achievability is obtained through a joint R\'enyi projection whose log likelihood ratio defines a single test with uniform error control over both hypothesis classes, without requiring the projected pair to be least favourable. For compact convex classes with full support on a finite alphabet, we determine the exact error exponents on both sides of the transition and show that the achievable exponent is attained at a unique R\'enyi order. The same framework recovers the fixed Type I composite Chernoff--Stein exponent and yields a polynomial refinement of the finite sample achievability result. We further identify conditions under which the projected pair is least favourable at finite sample size.
tldr: This paper presents finite sample bounds for composite hypothesis testing using Rényi divergences, identifying phase transitions and exact error exponents.
motivation: To obtain tight bounds on Type II error in composite testing with exponential Type I constraints.
method: Uses Rényi divergences and joint Rényi projections to define a single test with uniform error control.
result: Achieves exact error exponents on both sides of a phase transition and recovers known Chernoff-Stein exponents.
conclusion: Provides finite sample refinements and conditions for least favourable projections.

title: Horizon-Independent Contraction For Continuous-Time Discounted Regularized Mean-Field Games
authors: Junji Yan, U\u{g}ur Ayd{\i}n, Tamer Ba\c{s}ar
abstract: ArXiv:2608.27723v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study contraction properties of non-stationary continuous-time mean-field games (MFGs) under discounting and entropy regularization. The state of the representative agent evolves according to a controlled continuous-time Markov chain, and both the state and action spaces are finite. In contrast to the undiscounted case, we show that, under a sufficiently large discount rate, finite-horizon MFGs admit a horizon-independent contraction condition, which also coincides with the corresponding infinite-horizon non-stationary contraction condition. As a byproduct, we obtain an explicit convergence rate between finite- and infinite-horizon mean-field equilibria. For each finite horizon, we further derive a refined contraction criterion from the spectral radius of a positive operator that majorizes the propagation of policy errors, and show that its large-horizon limit agrees with the horizon-independent contraction factor. Finally, we provide an explicit error bound between discounted and undiscounted finite-horizon regularized equilibria.
tldr: This paper analyzes contraction properties for non-stationary continuous-time mean-field games under discounting and entropy regularization, deriving horizon-independent conditions and convergence rates.
motivation: To understand when finite-horizon mean-field games admit contraction properties that align with the infinite-horizon case, and to quantify the convergence of equilibria.
method: The study uses contraction analysis based on the spectral radius of a positive operator that propagates policy errors, and compares finite-horizon and infinite-horizon settings.
result: It shows that under a sufficiently large discount rate, finite-horizon MFGs have a horizon-independent contraction condition, and provides explicit convergence rates and error bounds between equilibria.
conclusion: The results offer theoretical guarantees for approximate equilibria in regularized mean-field games, which may have applications in multi-agent systems, but the topic is unrelated to the specified research interests.

title: Significance-Driven Semantic Communication
authors: Christian Mcdowell, Andrea Panebianco, Sirin Chakraborty, Yin Sun
abstract: ArXiv:2608.28441v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we study a significance-driven cross- layer semantic communication design problem. Based on sta- tistical decision theory, we introduce an information-theoretic measure of per-sample data significance that quantifies the task-specific value of each individual observation. Using this metric, we formulate a cross-layer optimization problem that simultaneously optimizes (i) physical-layer semantic encoding and inference and (ii) MAC-layer resource allocation, with the objective of maximizing semantic spectrum efficiency, defined as the semantic value delivered per unit bandwidth per unit time. At the physical layer, we develop Meta-Learning Variational Information Bottleneck (Meta-VIB), a new semantic transceiver that employs a meta-learned hypernetwork to compress high- dimensional observations into semantically significant latents, enabling instantaneous adaptation to dynamic channel conditions and varying symbol budgets without online retraining. At the MAC layer, we model channel allocation as a Multi-Action Restless Multi-Armed Bandit (MA-RMAB) and adopt the Q- Maximization algorithm, which dynamically allocates channel resources to sensors based on their semantic value of information. Experimental results on a real-world pedestrian safety dataset demonstrate that our joint design achieves substantial gains in semantic spectrum efficiency over baselines, reaching up to 1000 times gain at an average SNR of 0 dB and 40 times gain at an average SNR of 5 dB.
tldr: The paper proposes a cross-layer semantic communication design using information measures and resource allocation to maximize semantic spectrum efficiency.
motivation: To improve efficient communication by focusing on task-specific semantic value rather than raw data transmission.
method: Uses Meta-Learning Variational Information Bottleneck and Multi-Action Restless Multi-Armed Bandit for joint optimization of physical and MAC layers.
result: Achieves up to 1000x gain in semantic spectrum efficiency over baselines.
conclusion: Demonstrates significant improvements in semantic communication efficiency.

title: Quantum Information At Infinity
authors: L. Barbieri-Viale
abstract: ArXiv:2608.27498v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce the Quantum Information Space at Infinity (Quinfinity) [MATH] as the inverse limit of the symbolic Quantum [MATH]-Spaces [MATH], identified with the complete local real algebra of formal power series under the adic topology. The pure state pro-variety is formalized as the inverse limit of [MATH]-level pure state varieties, driven by the algebraic colimit of a direct system of real radical ideals. This real architecture internalizes the imaginary unit, collapsing the metric landscapes onto an invariant Riemannian isometry, which identifies the pro-variety directly with the classical Fisher-Rao statistical manifold. Within this framework, the Heisenberg uncertainty principle undergoes a structural regularization at infinity being intrinsically manifested as a localized truncation obstruction governed by adic algebraic derivations. Concurrently, the continuous Liouville-von Neumann equation operates as an internal derivation tangent to the pro-variety, while the open Gorini-Kossakowski-Sudarshan-Lindblad asymptotic master equation is intrinsically obtained via a non-associative symmetric Jordan product. This dissipative flow acts as a contracting radial vector field that dampens higher-order jet configurations, driving the state trajectories down the hierarchical tree toward the absolute zero element as a non-singular universal attractor.
tldr: Introduces a highly abstract mathematical framework 'Quinfinity' modeling quantum information spaces at infinity, linking algebraic geometry with the Fisher-Rao manifold and deriving dynamical equations from algebraic structures.
motivation: To provide a rigorous mathematical foundation for quantum information theory by constructing a limiting space that unifies state spaces and regularizes quantum uncertainties.
method: Uses inverse limits and pro-varieties over real radical ideals, internalizes the imaginary unit, and employs adic topology and Jordan algebras to derive dynamical equations.
result: Constructs a pro-variety identified with the Fisher-Rao manifold, regularizes the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, and derives both Liouville-von Neumann and Lindblad equations from geometric and algebraic principles.
conclusion: This framework offers a novel mathematical perspective on quantum information, but its practical implications for existing quantum information protocols are not yet clear.

title: Pulling Strings In Real Time: Flux Tube Dynamics In (2+1)-d $\mathbb{Z}_2$-Higgs Gauge Theories
authors: Zeno Bacciconi, Martina Frau, Luca Tagliacozzo, Michele Caselle, Marcello Dalmonte
abstract: ArXiv:2608.27561v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding real-time flux-tube dynamics in more than one spatial dimension is key to unlocking the non-perturbative physics of confinement, and is now actively pursued by quantum computing and simulation experiments. However, describing such dynamics has proven to be extremely challenging with both experiments and state-of-the-art numerical simulations limited to small volumes and short timescales. Here we investigate flux tube statics and real-time evolution in a genuine two-dimensional [MATH] Higgs gauge theory at system sizes and timescales order of magnitude beyond present experiments and numerics. The key enabling element is the recently introduced Clifford-augmented matrix product states (CAMPS) framework, which we demonstrate to parametrically reduce the entanglement that must be represented in the matrix product state; both in the pure-gauge limit and in the presence of dynamical matter. We benchmark this capability through stringent tests of effective string theory, including universal spectral features and flux tube roughening properties in presence of matter. We then introduce a string-pull protocol that selectively excites transverse modes and reconstructs their finite-size spectrum in real time. In the rough regime, the response is collective, and our simulations show that this is also well captured by universal effective string theory predictions. Strong confinement instead produces long-lived, lattice-locked local dynamics persisting to times [MATH]. These results provide ab initio evidence that effective string theory captures nonequilibrium string dynamics and reveal a hitherto unexplored long-lived prethermal regime of strongly confined flux tubes, providing a novel angle on how confinement dictates dynamics in more than one spatial dimension.
tldr: This paper uses Clifford-augmented matrix product states to simulate real-time flux tube dynamics in a (2+1)-dimensional Z2 Higgs gauge theory, revealing universal features and a long-lived prethermal regime.
motivation: Understanding real-time flux-tube dynamics in more than one spatial dimension is key for confinement physics, but it is challenging for experiments and numerics.
method: They employ the Clifford-augmented matrix product states (CAMPS) framework to reduce entanglement representation, enabling simulations at larger system sizes and timescales, and introduce a string-pull protocol to excite transverse modes.
result: They benchmark effective string theory predictions, show collective response in the rough regime, and find long-lived lattice-locked dynamics in strong confinement, revealing a prethermal regime.
conclusion: The results provide ab initio evidence for effective string theory in nonequilibrium string dynamics and offer a new perspective on confinement dynamics in higher dimensions.

title: Pulsed Single-photon Magnetometry With A $\Lambda$-type Three-level System: Near-optimal Frequency-resolved Photon Counting
authors: Seyed Mostafa Moniri, Elnaz Darsheshdar, Mikayel Khanbekyan
abstract: ArXiv:2608.27979v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate pulsed single-photon magnetometry with a Zeeman-sensitive [MATH]-type three-level system driven by a classical control field. We derive the asymptotic output state and decompose its quantum Fisher information into photon-loss, spectral-intensity, and spectral-phase contributions. Environmental coupling reshapes the scattering response and can increase magnetic-field information. At critical coupling, real-frequency zeros of the scattering amplitude redistribute information toward measurable spectral intensity, allowing frequency-resolved photon counting to capture nearly all of the magnetic-field information encoded in the output state when the zeros lie within the pulse bandwidth. For long Gaussian pulses with a smooth, nonzero central-frequency scattering amplitude, the additional spectral-intensity contribution and residual spectral-phase information gap decrease as [MATH] or faster.
tldr: This paper analyzes pulsed single-photon magnetometry using a three-level system, decomposing quantum Fisher information and showing that frequency-resolved photon counting can capture nearly all magnetic-field information under certain conditions.
motivation: To understand optimal extraction of magnetic-field information from scattered single photons in a three-level system.
method: Derive the asymptotic output state and decompose quantum Fisher information into photon-loss, spectral-intensity, and spectral-phase contributions; analyze environmental coupling and scattering zeros.
result: At critical coupling, frequency-resolved photon counting can capture almost all information when zeros are within the pulse bandwidth; for long Gaussian pulses, the additional spectral-intensity contribution and information gap decrease at a specified rate.
conclusion: The proposed method enables near-optimal magnetic-field information extraction via frequency-resolved photon counting.

title: Euler Topological Metals In 1d
authors: Jacob Shapiro Yichen Hu
abstract: ArXiv:2608.27554v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a rigorous one-dimensional formulation of Kane's transport proposal for probing the Euler characteristic of a Fermi sea. For a clean, translation-invariant continuum Hamiltonian with real-analytic dispersion, a Fermi sea confined to a finite momentum range, and nonzero Fermi velocity at every Fermi point, we analyze a particular Abel-regularized transport response (obtained by tracing over the Fermi sea) and prove that its large-time limit equals the Euler characteristic. We derive an explicit finite-time formula, show that quantization requires the large-time limit, and obtain a convergence rate under additional nonstationarity assumptions. We also prove the lattice analog, where the sharp commutator is trace-class and a completely filled band contributes zero. Finite-volume calculations illustrate the prescribed order of the thermodynamic and large-time limits.
tldr: The paper gives a rigorous one-dimensional formulation of Kane's proposal to probe the Euler characteristic of a Fermi sea via a transport response, proving its quantization in the large-time limit.
motivation: To provide a rigorous mathematical basis for using transport responses to extract topological invariants like the Euler characteristic of a Fermi sea in one-dimensional systems.
method: The authors analyze an Abel-regularized transport response for clean translation-invariant continuum and lattice Hamiltonians, proving that the large-time limit equals the Euler characteristic under assumptions of real-analytic dispersion and nonzero Fermi velocity.
result: They derive an explicit finite-time formula, show that quantization requires the large-time limit, and obtain a convergence rate under additional nonstationarity assumptions. They also prove the lattice analog where the commutator is trace-class and a filled band contributes zero.
conclusion: The paper establishes a rigorous connection between transport response and the Euler characteristic of the Fermi sea, with implications for topological metals, but is outside the user's research focus.

title: Plateau-Constrained Selection Of Commuting Phase-Term Orderings Under A Fixed Maintained-Parity Compiler Contract
authors: Owen Friedewald, Ali Shiri Sichani, Chi-Ren Shyu
abstract: ArXiv:2608.27592v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ordering objectives for commuting phase terms can have many equal optima, yet prior methods do not characterize or exploit those ties. We use a classical two-stage permutation search under fixed placement and maintained-parity quantum lowering: Stage 1 certifies the primary support optimum, and Stage 2 samples equal-cost tours and selects by a frozen routed score. On synthetic 16-qubit assignment-Ising instances, exact counting through 20 terms establishes instance-dependent multiplicity; when the support lower bound is attained, the reversal-reduced width equals the number of undirected Hamiltonian paths of the support line graph. A revised engineering analysis found 9.14% fewer routed controlled-NOT gates than unoptimized order, while the registered comparison found 11.10% fewer than prior stochastic search. Among 24 sampled minimum-support-cost orders at 36 terms, direct-depth selection reduced opposite-SABRE-seed depth by 12.83% in all 20 aggregates, whereas a matched 24-restart control changed depth by only -0.41% (unresolved). Candidate rankings persisted across SABRE routing seeds, explaining why selection survived routing re-randomization. The depth benefit transferred to a second generator and to 48 terms, but reversed under BasicSwap. On a prospective IBM Heron panel, raw generator error shifted by -0.0025 (-0.59%); fixed-panel shot uncertainty excluded zero, but term-seed inference remained unresolved. Equal-primary-cost tours are a useful router-conditioned compiler freedom, not a guaranteed hardware benefit.
tldr: A quantum compiler optimization method that selects among equal-cost orderings of commuting phase terms to reduce CNOT gates and improve routing depth.
motivation: Existing methods do not exploit ties in ordering objectives for commuting phase terms, which can have many equal optima that may affect circuit quality.
method: A classical two-stage permutation search under fixed placement and maintained-parity quantum lowering: stage 1 certifies the primary support optimum, and stage 2 samples equal-cost tours and selects by a frozen routed score.
result: On synthetic 16-qubit instances, found 9.14% fewer routed CNOT gates than unoptimized order and 11.10% fewer than prior stochastic search; depth benefit of 12.83% across 20 aggregates at 36 terms, but reversed under BasicSwap.
conclusion: Equal-primary-cost tours are a useful router-conditioned compiler freedom, but not a guaranteed hardware benefit.

title: Quantum SEDONet: Spectrally-Embedded Quantum Deep Operator Networks For Partial Differential Equations
authors: Muhammad Abid, Arth Sojitra, Bipin Tiwari, Omer San
abstract: ArXiv:2608.27626v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum DeepONet accelerates neural-operator inference by evaluating an orthogonally parameterized network on a quantum computer, reproducing in ideal simulation the accuracy of its classical counterpart at asymptotically lower inference cost. Its trunk network, however, receives query coordinates with limited spectral structure, requiring the network to learn oscillatory features through its nonlinearities. We propose Quantum SEDONet (Spectral-Embedded Deep Operator Network), which assigns each trunk coordinate a spectral basis according to its boundary condition: Fourier features for periodic coordinates and Chebyshev features for bounded, non-periodic coordinates. The basis is selected per coordinate rather than per problem, allowing both representations within a single problem. Under unary amplitude encoding, the embedding incurs no additional qubits or circuit depth when its dimension remains within the network width, while increasing the parameter count by only a few percent. Across four benchmarks, Quantum SEDONet reduces the mean relative L2 error by 54.1% for the antiderivative, 49.6% for advection, 36.0% for Burgers, and 36.2% for a mixed-boundary channel Poisson problem. Quantum and classical evaluation paths agree to within 10^-8 throughout. The channel Poisson problem simultaneously uses Fourier features in the periodic direction and Chebyshev features in the bounded direction, demonstrating coordinate-wise boundary-matched spectral embedding without additional quantum-resource cost.
tldr: Quantum SEDONet embeds spectral features (Fourier/Chebyshev) into quantum operator networks to improve PDE accuracy, reducing errors by 36-54% without additional quantum resources in ideal simulation.
motivation: Quantum DeepONet aims for faster inference but trunk coordinates lack spectral structure, forcing the network to learn oscillatory features via nonlinearities; spectral embedding is proposed to boost accuracy.
method: Each trunk coordinate is assigned a spectral basis (Fourier for periodic, Chebyshev for bounded) based on boundary conditions, embedded without adding qubits or depth when within network width, and tested on four PDE benchmarks.
result: Quantum SEDONet reduces mean relative L2 error by 54.1% for antiderivative, 49.6% for advection, 36.0% for Burgers, and 36.2% for mixed-boundary channel Poisson, with quantum-classical agreement within 10^-8.
conclusion: Coordinate-wise spectral embedding significantly improves quantum operator network accuracy at minimal extra cost, showcasing boundary-condition-aware design for quantum PDE solvers.

title: Fractional Hall Conductance Of Laughlin States From A Topological Index
authors: Sven Bachmann, Severin Schraven, Jacob Shapiro, Simone Warzel
abstract: ArXiv:2608.27767v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We provide a rigorous Laughlin-pump argument that establishes the fractional quantization of the Hall conductance directly from the Laughlin state as a topological index. Our proof uses a recently defined index of a pair of pure states together with an infinite matrix product state analysis that is rigorous on a sufficiently thin cylinder. By virtue of the connection to an index, our result implies, in particular, that Laughlin states are representatives of topologically stable fractional quantum Hall phases.
tldr: This paper rigorously establishes the fractional quantization of Hall conductance for Laughlin states using a topological index and matrix product state analysis on thin cylinders.
motivation: To provide a rigorous proof of the fractional Hall conductance quantization directly from Laughlin states as a topological index, and to show the topological stability of these phases.
method: The authors use a recently defined index of a pair of pure states together with an infinite matrix product state analysis that is rigorous on a sufficiently thin cylinder.
result: They establish the fractional quantization of the Hall conductance as a topological index and conclude that Laughlin states are representatives of topologically stable fractional quantum Hall phases.
conclusion: The result confirms the topological robustness of Laughlin states in fractional quantum Hall systems.

title: Vectorized Symmetric And Fermionic Tensor Network Implementations For GPU-Accelerated Variational Monte Carlo
authors: Si-Jing Du, Johnnie Gray, Ao Chen, Garnet Kin-Lic Chan
abstract: ArXiv:2608.27861v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Variational Monte Carlo (VMC) calculations based on tensor networks (TN) have recently achieved competitive accuracy in ground-state calculations of strongly correlated spin and fermionic systems. However, existing tensor network VMC (TN-VMC) algorithms have not been formulated in a manner that can fully utilize GPU acceleration. We tackle the key missing ingredient, namely, the vectorized evaluation of tensor network amplitudes and tensor network operations. This ensures high GPU utilization by batching over computations with identical structure. In particular, we show how to achieve vectorization for the practically relevant case of abelian symmetric tensor networks (which includes fermionic tensor networks) by developing a ``flat'' tensor network formalism for block-sparse tensor representation and contraction. Using this, we construct a GPU-adapted symmetric TN-VMC workflow with batched tensor network computation. In the two-dimensional Fermi--Hubbard model, we demonstrate a GPU speedup of up to [MATH] over single core CPU implementations, for fermionic TN variational wavefunctions.
tldr: This paper presents vectorized implementations of symmetric and fermionic tensor networks for GPU-accelerated variational Monte Carlo, achieving significant speedups in the Fermi-Hubbard model.
motivation: Existing tensor network VMC algorithms do not fully utilize GPU acceleration; the authors aim to address this by developing a vectorized flat tensor network formalism for block-sparse tensors.
method: They develop a 'flat' tensor network formalism for abelian symmetric tensor networks, enabling batched tensor operations on GPUs, and then construct a GPU-adapted symmetric TN-VMC workflow.
result: They demonstrate a GPU speedup of up to [MATH] (presumably a large factor) over single core CPU implementations for fermionic TN variational wavefunctions in the 2D Fermi-Hubbard model.
conclusion: The vectorization approach enables efficient GPU utilization for tensor network VMC, potentially advancing simulations of strongly correlated systems.

title: Holomorphy Of The Ground State And Energy For Bosonic Quadratic Hamiltonians
authors: Kota Imura, Shinnosuke Izumi, Yasumichi Matsuzawa, Itaru Sasaki
abstract: ArXiv:2608.27862v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the holomorphy of the ground state and its energy with respect to the coupling constant for bosonic quadratic Hamiltonians. We prove general theorems establishing this holomorphy, thereby providing a rigorous justification for formal perturbative expansions. This theory is applied to several concrete models, including the single pair interaction model and the Pauli-Fierz model in the dipole approximation. Importantly, for the Pauli-Fierz model with a realistic ultraviolet cutoff, the perturbation expansions in the elementary charge converge at the physical charge value, even when mass renormalization is taken into account. Furthermore, we explicitly determine the radii of convergence of the ground states and their energies for both the single pair interaction model and the fibers of the translation-invariant Pauli-Fierz model.
tldr: The paper proves holomorphy of ground states and energies for bosonic quadratic Hamiltonians, justifying perturbative expansions, with applications to specific models including the Pauli-Fierz model.
motivation: To rigorously justify formal perturbative expansions in quantum field theory models with bosonic quadratic Hamiltonians.
method: The authors establish general theorems demonstrating holomorphy in the coupling constant, then apply them to concrete models like the single pair interaction and Pauli-Fierz models, computing radii of convergence.
result: They prove convergence of perturbation expansions for the Pauli-Fierz model at the physical charge value even with mass renormalization, and explicitly determine convergence radii for the models.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous mathematical foundation for perturbative expansions in these bosonic systems, but is not directly related to the specified research directions.

title: Density-gradient Effect In High-harmonic Generation In Gases
authors: Zolt\'an Filus, T\'imea Gr\'osz, Chinmoy Biswas, L\'en\'ard Guly\'as Oldal, Tam\'as Bartyik, Barnab\'as Gilicze, Subhendu Kahaly, Katalin Varj\'u, Bal\'azs Major
abstract: ArXiv:2608.28032v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-harmonic generation (HHG) in gaseous targets is the most widespread method to produce coherent extreme-ultraviolet (XUV) pulses with sub-femtosecond duration. However, this process has intrinsically low efficiency, and substantial research and development is devoted worldwide to increase the achievable photon flux through this highly nonlinear light--matter interaction process. In this work, we show the strong interplay of phase matching and absorption in gas-pressure gradients, substantially affecting macroscopic HHG efficiency. Through detailed experimental analysis and supporting numerical studies, we highlight their significance, particularly at the boundaries of the interaction volume. The concluded results have implications in the massively expanding application possibilities of HHG sources requiring high photon flux, for example in the semiconductor industry, in nanoscale imaging of biological and industrial samples, or in nonlinear optics in the XUV regime.
tldr: This paper studies how gas density gradients affect high-harmonic generation efficiency through phase matching and absorption, especially at interaction boundaries.
motivation: To increase the low intrinsic efficiency of high-harmonic generation sources for applications requiring high photon flux.
method: Experimental measurements combined with numerical simulations analyze the impact of gas-pressure gradients on phase matching and absorption in HHG.
result: The interplay of phase matching and absorption in pressure gradients substantially affects HHG efficiency, most notably at the boundaries of the interaction volume.
conclusion: Optimizing density gradients could improve HHG photon flux, benefiting applications like semiconductor lithography and nanoscale imaging.

title: A Synthetic Iterative Scheme For Non-Gray Phonon Boltzmann Transport Equation With Dual Relaxation Times
authors: Dingtao Shen, Jia Liu, Wei Su
abstract: ArXiv:2608.28101v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Solving the non-gray Callaway phonon Boltzmann transport equation allows a dual-relaxation-time approximation of separate normal and resistive scatterings and resolving the mode-dependent spectrum. The conventional iterative scheme (CIS) for deterministic solutions avoids a monolithic phase-space inversion, but its collision-source iteration can become prohibitively slow at a large characteristic length of a material. Existing synthetic acceleration schemes address either non-gray single-relaxation models or gray dual-relaxation models, leaving mode-resolved dual-relaxation transport without a dedicated acceleration framework. We develop a general synthetic iterative scheme (GSIS) for the stationary, linearized, non-gray Callaway equation, where synthetic approximations for the normal-process pseudo-temperature and phonon drift velocity are provided by exact energy and quasi-momentum balance laws closed with first-order Chapman-Enskog constitutive relations and non-equilibrium terms evaluated from the kinetic solution. The resistive-process pseudo-temperature is retrieved from the two quantities. Each iteration couples an upwind nodal discontinuous Galerkin kinetic sweep and a hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin solution of the synthetic equations to achieve high-order spatial discretization. A branch- and frequency-resolved Fourier analysis identifies the deterioration of CIS and shows that the GSIS contraction factor remains bounded away from unity for the considered graphene material. Asymptotic analysis indicates that GSIS reduces to a consistent discretization of a Guyer-Krumhansl-like equation and Fourier's law of heat conduction in the hydrodynamic and diffusive limits, respectively.
tldr: This paper develops a general synthetic iterative scheme (GSIS) to accelerate the solution of the non-gray phonon Boltzmann transport equation with dual relaxation times.
motivation: The conventional iterative scheme (CIS) becomes prohibitively slow for large characteristic lengths, and existing acceleration methods do not handle mode-resolved dual-relaxation transport.
method: The GSIS introduces synthetic approximations for normal-process pseudo-temperature and phonon drift velocity derived from exact energy and quasi-momentum balance laws with Chapman-Enskog constitutive relations, and couples an upwind nodal discontinuous Galerkin kinetic sweep with a hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin solution of the synthetic equations.
result: The GSIS contraction factor remains bounded away from unity, improving convergence over CIS, and asymptotic analysis shows it reduces to a Guyer-Krumhansl-like equation in the hydrodynamic limit and Fourier's law in the diffusive limit.
conclusion: The scheme provides a consistent and efficient acceleration for non-gray dual-relaxation phonon transport, applicable to materials like graphene.

title: Explicit Bound States And Threshold Resonances For Two Identical Fermions On A One-Dimensional Lattice
authors: Shakhobiddin I. Khamidov Sobir S. Ulashov
abstract: ArXiv:2608.28125v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a two-particle lattice Schr\"odinger operator describing two identical fermions on the one-dimensional lattice [MATH] with nearest-neighbor interaction of strength [MATH]. Using the direct-integral decomposition with respect to the total quasi-momentum [MATH], we reduce the problem to fiber operators [MATH] acting in the odd relative-coordinate space. For [MATH], the essential spectrum is \[ \sigma_{}(H_\lambda(k)) = [4-4\cos(k/2),\,4+4\cos(k/2)]. \] We give a complete description of the spectral transition at both edges. The operator has a unique simple eigenvalue outside the essential spectrum if and only if \[ |\lambda|>2\cos(k/2), \] in which case \[ E(k,\lambda) = 4+\lambda+{\lambda}. \] For [MATH] there is no discrete eigenvalue. At the critical coupling [MATH], the eigenvalue merges with the corresponding spectral edge and becomes a threshold resonance, with a bounded non-square-integrable odd solution. We also derive the threshold and strong-coupling asymptotics of the eigenvalue and eigenfunction. In the strong-coupling regime the eigenfunction localizes at the interaction sites, whereas at critical coupling it converges pointwise to the corresponding resonant solution. The exceptional fiber [MATH], where the hopping vanishes and the essential spectrum collapses to [MATH], is treated separately.
tldr: The paper analyzes a two-fermion lattice Schrödinger operator, deriving explicit bound state conditions and threshold resonance behavior.
motivation: To understand the spectral properties of two identical fermions on a one-dimensional lattice with nearest-neighbor interaction.
method: Uses direct-integral decomposition and fiber operators to study the spectrum and eigenfunctions.
result: Provides complete description of spectral edges, eigenvalue existence criteria, and asymptotics.
conclusion: The dynamics of the system are characterized by coupling strength, with threshold resonances occurring at critical coupling.

title: Performance Optimization Of Short Reach Optical Interconnects Based On Direct Detection
authors: Luca Po\`i, Stella Civelli, Marco Secondini, Li Zhang, Dario Cellini, Asfand Nizamani, Ramin Solaimani, Lorenzo de Marinis, Mareli Rodigheri, Pantea Nadimi Goki, Muhammad A. Naz, Giampiero Contestabile, Enrico Forestieri, Fabio Cavaliere
abstract: ArXiv:2608.28129v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Short-reach optical interconnects are evolving toward data rates beyond 400 Gb/s per lane, driven by the bandwidth and energy-efficiency requirements of AI-enabled datacenter networks. At these operating speeds, channel impairments, device nonlinearities, and hardware constraints limit the effectiveness of conventional transceiver design and digital signal processing (DSP). This paper presents a unified framework for the optimization of direct-detection optical interconnects, encompassing digital surrogate modeling, receiver-side DSP optimization, and end-to-end (E2E) transceiver learning. The proposed formulation provides a common perspective for model-based and machine-learning-based approaches, including linear and nonlinear equalization, lookup tables, decision trees, neural-network receivers, and E2E optimization. Their performance is discussed together with computational complexity and hardware implementation aspects, highlighting the associated trade-offs. We show, through simulations and experimental validations, that for a 40~Gb/s 10~km link, decision trees can outperform by 0.5--1~dB conventional linear equalization, with negligible hardware requirements. Moreover, we show that an E2E technique based on transformers can provide a gain up to 6~dB, highlighting the potential of joint transceiver optimization to improve the performance of next-generation short-reach optical links.
tldr: This paper presents a unified framework for optimizing short-reach optical interconnects using direct detection, combining model-based and machine-learning approaches.
motivation: The demand for higher data rates in AI-enabled datacenter networks pushes short-reach optical interconnects beyond 400 Gb/s per lane, where conventional transceiver design and DSP become limited by channel impairments and hardware constraints.
method: The authors propose a unified optimization framework that includes digital surrogate modeling, receiver-side DSP optimization, and end-to-end transceiver learning, comparing linear and nonlinear equalization, decision trees, neural networks, and transformer-based E2E approaches.
result: Simulations and experiments on a 40 Gb/s 10 km link show decision trees outperform linear equalization by 0.5–1 dB with negligible hardware requirements, while a transformer-based E2E technique provides up to 6 dB gain.
conclusion: The results highlight the potential of joint transceiver optimization and machine learning to improve next-generation short-reach optical links.

title: Algebraic Implicitization Techniques In The Graphical Models Program
authors: Liam Solus
abstract: ArXiv:2608.27636v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many aspects of daily life now rely on technology driven by advanced techniques for analyzing multivariate data. Graphical models provide the general framework within which much of these analyses take place. However, different data types require different graphical models, with each requiring its own basic mathematical theory to guide sound statistical inference. Developing this theory for a family of graphical models requires solutions to fundamental questions, where emerging mathematical approaches are utilizing what can collectively be called algebraic implicitization techniques. These notes provide an introduction to the basics of graphical models and the algebraic implicitization techniques now appearing in instances of the graphical models program.
tldr: This paper introduces graphical models and algebraic implicitization techniques used in the graphical models program.
motivation: To develop mathematical theories for different graphical models to guide sound statistical inference.
method: The notes provide an introduction to the basics of graphical models and the algebraic implicitization techniques.
result: The paper presents an overview of how algebraic implicitization can be applied to graphical models.
conclusion: These techniques are emerging as useful for solving fundamental questions in graphical models.

title: Numerical Analysis Of Data Assimilation For Slightly Compressible Flow
authors: Rui Fang Aytekin \c{c}{\i}b{\i}k
abstract: ArXiv:2608.27647v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continuous data assimilation improves flow predictions by continually nudging a model toward available observational data. For slightly compressible flow, a recent model addresses the limitations of velocity-only nudging by assimilating both velocity and pressure data and nudging both quantities into the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations [5]; continuous-in-time error estimates and preliminary experiments show that this joint nudging is effective and substantially reduces the model error relative to velocity-only nudging. Motivated by these results, we carry out the numerical analysis of the model and its finite element discretizations.
